header:
Big Tech's AI bill
What it means for you

lines.text: Meta's AI bill is now bigger than the cash it makes.
lines.say: Meta's AI bill is now bigger than the cash it makes.

lines.text: July to Sept 2026: Meta spent $34.9B on capex. Its business brought in $32.8B.
lines.say: From July through September, Meta spent thirty-four point nine billion dollars on capex, while its business brought in thirty-two point eight billion.

lines.text: That gap is called free cash flow: -$2.12B for Meta in Q3.
lines.say: That gap has a name, free cash flow, and for Meta it came out to negative two point one two billion dollars.

lines.text: Investors noticed. Meta's stock fell nearly 7% on Oct 22.
lines.say: Investors noticed. Meta's stock fell nearly seven percent on October twenty-second.

lines.text: And Meta wasn't alone. Tesla and SpaceX told versions of the same story within about a day.
lines.say: And Meta wasn't alone. Tesla and SpaceX told versions of the same story within about a day.

lines.text: By spring 2026 tallies, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta planned over $700B of 2026 capex.
lines.say: Zoom out, and spring tallies had Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta planning more than seven hundred billion dollars of capital spending in twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Many analysts compare it to an earlier boom: the late-1990s telecom and fiber build-out.
lines.say: Plenty of analysts compare that to one earlier boom: the late nineteen-nineties race to wire the world with fiber.

lines.text: That one ended with the Nasdaq down 78% from its peak.
lines.say: That one ended with the Nasdaq down seventy-eight percent from its peak.

lines.text: So is the AI bill a smart bet or a 1999 rerun? Nobody knows yet. But the numbers tell a story.
lines.say: So is the AI bill a smart bet, or a nineteen ninety-nine rerun? Nobody knows yet. But the numbers tell a story.

lines.text: Coming up: the bills, the size, the 1990s lesson, who wins, and your money.
lines.say: Here's the plan: the bills, the nineties lesson, who wins and who pays, and what it means for your money.

lines.text: Chapter 1: Three big bills
lines.say: Let's start with three companies and three very big bills.

lines.text: Meta reported on Oct 21: sales up 26% to $64.6B. The ad business is doing fine.
lines.say: Meta reported on October twenty-first. Sales rose twenty-six percent, to sixty-four point six billion dollars, so the ad business is doing just fine.

lines.text: The issue is the spending. Meta's capex by year, including finance leases, from its own reports.
lines.say: The issue is the spending. Here's Meta's capital spending, year by year, straight from its own reports.
Thirty-two billion in twenty twenty-two, twenty-eight in twenty twenty-three, thirty-nine in twenty twenty-four, then seventy-two point two billion in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Q3 2026 alone: $34.91B. That's more than Meta spent in all of 2023.
lines.say: In the third quarter alone, Meta spent thirty-four point nine one billion dollars, more than in all of twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Its plan for all of 2026: $135B to $145B.
lines.say: And its plan for all of twenty twenty-six is one hundred thirty-five to one hundred forty-five billion dollars.

lines.text: Free cash flow had already shrunk to $784M in Q2, down 91% from a year earlier.
lines.say: Its free cash flow had already shrunk to seven hundred eighty-four million dollars in the second quarter, down ninety-one percent in a year.

lines.text: Meta also announced non-voting Class C shares. Its board named raising capital, employee pay and deals as uses.
lines.say: Meta also announced new Class C shares with no votes. Its board said they could help raise capital, pay employees and fund deals.

lines.text: Same evening, Tesla: sales about flat at roughly $28B, profit down 43% to $787M.
lines.say: That same evening, Tesla reported sales roughly flat at about twenty-eight billion dollars, and profit down forty-three percent, to seven hundred eighty-seven million.

lines.text: Meanwhile, research spending jumped 69% to $2.76B.
lines.say: Meanwhile, its research and development spending jumped sixty-nine percent, to two point seven six billion dollars.

lines.text: Tesla says that money goes into AI, its Optimus robot and new vehicles, and that it will weigh on profit.
lines.say: Tesla says that money goes into AI, its Optimus robot and new vehicles, and that it will weigh on profit.

lines.text: Tesla's operating margin: 2.6%, about $2.60 of operating profit per $100 of sales.
lines.say: Its operating margin was two point six percent, about two dollars and sixty cents of operating profit per hundred dollars of sales.

lines.text: SpaceX, on Oct 20: its AI unit is now its biggest business by sales, at $7.56B.
lines.say: And SpaceX, on October twentieth, said its AI unit is now its biggest business by sales, at seven point five six billion dollars.

lines.text: SpaceX's total revenue jumped 161% to $14.58B.
lines.say: Overall, its revenue jumped a hundred sixty-one percent, to fourteen point five eight billion dollars.

lines.text: But Starlink made $2.37B of operating profit, about 85% of the total, vs $431M for AI.
lines.say: But the profit came from elsewhere. Starlink made two point three seven billion dollars of operating profit, about eighty-five percent of the total, versus four hundred thirty-one million for AI.

lines.text: SpaceX says the AI figure includes about $1.2B of stock pay tied to its Cursor deal. Still, satellites paid the bills.
lines.say: SpaceX says the AI number includes about one point two billion dollars of stock pay from its Cursor deal. Still, satellites paid the bills.

lines.text: Three companies, one pattern: spend big on AI now, hope the profits show up later.
lines.say: So, three companies, one pattern: spend heavily on AI now, and hope the profits show up later.

lines.text: Chapter 2: How big is the bill?
lines.say: Now let's zoom out and see how big this bill really is.

lines.text: Capex = money spent on big, lasting things: data centers, servers, networks.
lines.say: First, a definition. Capex, or capital expenditures, is money spent on big, long-lasting things like data centers, servers and networks.

lines.text: Free cash flow = cash from the business minus capex. It pays for dividends, buybacks and a cushion.
lines.say: Free cash flow is what's left: cash from the business, minus capex. It pays for dividends, buybacks and a safety cushion.

lines.text: Meta, Q3 2026: $32.79B in, minus $34.91B of capex, leaves -$2.12B.
lines.say: For Meta's third quarter: thirty-two point seven nine billion dollars in, minus thirty-four point nine one billion of capex, leaves negative two point one two billion.

lines.text: Alphabet hit the same wall earlier: free cash flow of about -$5.9B in Q2 2026, Reuters reported.
lines.say: Alphabet, Google's parent, hit the same wall a quarter earlier. Reuters reported free cash flow of about negative five point nine billion dollars in the second quarter.

lines.text: Its Q2 capex: $44.9B, about double a year earlier.
lines.say: That's because its capex in that quarter reached forty-four point nine billion dollars, roughly double a year earlier.

lines.text: Add up the 4 giants: spring tallies put 2026 plans above $700B, up from about $410B in 2025.
lines.say: Add up the four giants, and spring tallies put twenty twenty-six plans above seven hundred billion dollars, up from about four hundred ten billion in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: That's more than $1.9B every single day ($700B / 365).
lines.say: That works out to more than one point nine billion dollars, every single day of the year.

lines.text: Where does it come from? Mostly from their giant businesses. But more and more, from borrowing.
lines.say: So where does all that money come from? Mostly from their giant businesses. But more and more, from borrowing.

lines.text: BofA: Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle sold $121B of US bonds in 2025.
lines.say: Bank of America counts a hundred twenty-one billion dollars of US bonds sold in twenty twenty-five by Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle.

lines.text: In 2020-24 they averaged $28B a year. That's more than 4x the old pace.
lines.say: From twenty twenty to twenty twenty-four, they averaged twenty-eight billion a year. So that's more than four times the old pace.

lines.text: Meta's own $30B bond in Oct 2025 was the largest non-merger high-grade sale on record, per MUFG.
lines.say: Meta's own thirty billion dollar bond in October twenty twenty-five was the biggest non-merger high-grade sale on record, per the bank MUFG.

lines.text: 2026 looks bigger still: in March, BofA raised its 2026 forecast for these bond sales to $175B.
lines.say: And twenty twenty-six looks even bigger. In March, Bank of America raised its forecast for big cloud companies' bond sales this year to a hundred seventy-five billion dollars.

lines.text: Borrowing huge sums to build a network everyone says the future needs. Sound familiar?
lines.say: Borrowing huge sums to build a network everyone says the future needs. If that sounds familiar, there's a reason.

lines.text: Chapter 3: We've seen this before
lines.say: Let's rewind to the nineteen-nineties.

lines.text: 1996: the Telecommunications Act opened phone and internet markets to new competition.
lines.say: In nineteen ninety-six, the Telecommunications Act opened phone and internet markets to new competition.

lines.text: Telecom companies then invested more than $500B, mostly borrowed, by one widely cited estimate.
lines.say: Telecom companies then poured more than five hundred billion dollars, mostly borrowed, into fiber, switches and wireless networks, by one widely cited estimate.

lines.text: The popular claim: internet traffic doubled every 3 months. Researcher Andrew Odlyzko found it was closer to once a year.
lines.say: Back then, a popular claim said internet traffic doubled every three months. Researcher Andrew Odlyzko showed it was closer to once a year.

lines.text: Still fast, just not that fast. By the bust, only about 10% of 39 million miles of US fiber was in use, per a Merrill Lynch estimate.
lines.say: Still fast, just not that fast. When the bubble burst, a Merrill Lynch estimate found only about ten percent of America's thirty-nine million miles of fiber in use.

lines.text: Stocks rode it up and down. The Nasdaq at each year-end, 1997 to 2002.
lines.say: Stocks rode it up, then down. Here's the Nasdaq at each year-end, from nineteen ninety-seven to two thousand two.

lines.text: 1,570 at the end of 1997, 4,069 in 1999, then 1,336 by the end of 2002.
lines.say: Fifteen hundred seventy at the end of ninety-seven, four thousand sixty-nine in ninety-nine, then thirteen hundred thirty-six by the end of two thousand two.

lines.text: Record close: 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000. By October 2002, it was down 78%.
lines.say: Its record close was five thousand forty-eight point six two, on March tenth, two thousand. By October two thousand two, it was down seventy-eight percent.

lines.text: It took until April 2015, about 15 years, to get back above that high.
lines.say: And it took until April twenty fifteen, about fifteen years, for the Nasdaq to get back above that high.

lines.text: Jan 2002: Global Crossing went bankrupt with $12.4B of debt.
lines.say: Meanwhile, the builders broke. In January two thousand two, Global Crossing went bankrupt, with twelve point four billion dollars of debt.

lines.text: July 2002: WorldCom, then the biggest US bankruptcy ever, after an $11B accounting fraud.
lines.say: Then in July, WorldCom filed what was then the biggest bankruptcy in US history, after an eleven billion dollar accounting fraud.

lines.text: The twist: the fiber didn't disappear. It was sold cheap, and it carried much of the internet's later growth.
lines.say: Here's the twist. The fiber didn't disappear. Buyers got it for a fraction of its cost, and it carried much of the internet's later growth.

lines.text: The big difference: 1990s builders ran mostly on debt. Today's spenders have huge profitable businesses, though borrowing is rising.
lines.say: The big difference: nineties builders ran mostly on debt. Today's spenders have giant, profitable businesses and cash piles, though their borrowing is climbing.

lines.text: Example: Meta had $82.45B in cash and marketable securities on Sept 30, 2026.
lines.say: Meta, for example, had eighty-two point four five billion dollars in cash and marketable securities at the end of September.

lines.text: The lesson from 2000: a technology can be real, and many who paid to build it can still lose.
lines.say: So the lesson isn't that the internet was fake. It's that a technology can win while many people who paid to build it lose.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Who wins, who pays
lines.say: So who's actually getting all this money, and who's paying for it?

lines.text: Nvidia, the AI chipmaker: $96.2B in sales in the quarter ended July 26, 2026, up 106%.
lines.say: Start with the shovel seller. Nvidia's sales hit ninety-six point two billion dollars in the quarter ended July twenty-sixth, up a hundred and six percent.

lines.text: Its data center business alone: $89.0B, up 117%.
lines.say: Its data center business alone brought in eighty-nine billion dollars, up a hundred and seventeen percent.

lines.text: Nvidia's net income that quarter: $59.7B.
lines.say: And its net income that quarter was fifty-nine point seven billion dollars.

lines.text: The key idea: one company's capex is another company's revenue.
lines.say: That's the key idea here. One company's capex is another company's revenue.

lines.text: Getting paid: chipmakers, data center builders, power gear makers. Paying now: the spenders and their shareholders.
lines.say: The money flows to chipmakers, data center builders and power equipment makers. The spenders pay now, in thinner cash flow, while shareholders wait.

lines.text: Bond buyers are in this too: they're lending a growing share of the money.
lines.say: Bond buyers are in this too. They're the ones lending a growing share of the money.

lines.text: That's why Meta's stock fell nearly 7% on Oct 22, even though sales jumped 26%.
lines.say: And that's why Meta's stock fell nearly seven percent on October twenty-second, even though its sales jumped twenty-six percent.

lines.text: Many investors are asking one question: when does the spending pay for itself?
lines.say: Many investors are asking one question: when does all this spending start paying for itself?

lines.text: The honest answer: the bill is certain. The payoff isn't, at least not yet.
lines.say: Here's the honest version. The bill is certain. The payoff isn't, at least not yet.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Your money, what's next
lines.say: Now, why should you care if you've never bought a single tech stock?

lines.text: The 10 biggest stocks were about 39.1% of the S&P 500 on Sept 30, 2026 (S&P Dow Jones Indices data, as reported).
lines.say: If you own an S and P five hundred index fund, maybe in a four oh one K, the ten biggest companies were about thirty-nine point one percent of it at the end of September.

lines.text: That's called concentration: a few stocks carry a big share of the index.
lines.say: That's called concentration: a few stocks carry a big share of the whole index.

lines.text: Before the dot-com bust, the top 10's weight peaked around 26%, by one market analysis.
lines.say: Before the dot-com bust, the top ten peaked around twenty-six percent, by one market analysis. Today's index leans even harder on its giants.

lines.text: Example: $10,000 in an S&P 500 fund means about $3,910 sits in its 10 biggest companies.
lines.say: In a simple example, ten thousand dollars in an S and P five hundred fund puts about three thousand nine hundred ten dollars in those ten companies.

lines.text: Just an example: index weights move every day with prices.
lines.say: That's just an example, since the weights move every day with prices.

lines.text: Many of those 10 are the AI spenders themselves, plus Nvidia, the chipmaker selling to them.
lines.say: And many of those ten are the AI spenders themselves, plus Nvidia, the chipmaker selling to them.

lines.text: So whether the AI bet pays off or not, an index fund holder is already in it.
lines.say: So whether the AI bet pays off or not, an index fund holder is already along for the ride.

lines.text: Every dollar of a company's cash has a few possible jobs. A growing share now goes to data centers.
lines.say: Think of a company's cash as having a few possible jobs. Right now, a growing share goes into data centers.

lines.text: That can leave less for buybacks, dividends or a cushion, unless a company borrows or sells more shares. Raising capital is one use Meta's board named for Class C.
lines.say: That can leave less for buybacks, dividends or a cushion, unless a company borrows or sells more shares. Raising capital is one use Meta's board named for Class C.

lines.text: None of this is a signal to buy or sell. It's how to read the headlines and know what you own.
lines.say: None of this is a signal to buy or sell anything. It's just how to read the headlines, and know what you already own.

lines.text: What's next: Wed, Oct 28, after the close, Alphabet and Microsoft report.
lines.say: So what's next? On Wednesday, October twenty-eighth, after the market closes, Alphabet and Microsoft both report.

lines.text: Same day: the Fed announces its interest rate decision.
lines.say: That same day, the Federal Reserve announces its next interest rate decision.

lines.text: The Fed's range is 3.75%-4.00% after its Sept 16, 2026 hike.
lines.say: The Fed's target range is three point seven five to four percent, after a hike on September sixteenth.

lines.text: Thursday, Oct 29: Amazon.
lines.say: On Thursday, October twenty-ninth, it's Amazon's turn.

lines.text: Monday, Nov 2: Apple, in John Ternus's first earnings call as CEO.
lines.say: And on Monday, November second, Apple reports, in John Ternus's first earnings call as CEO.

lines.text: Jan 19, 2027: Meta's charter change takes effect and Class C shares are handed out.
lines.say: Further out, on January nineteenth, twenty twenty-seven, Meta's charter change takes effect and its new Class C shares get handed out.

lines.text: In each report, watch capex plans and cloud sales growth.
lines.say: In each report, watch two numbers first: whether capex plans rise again, and whether cloud sales are keeping up.

lines.text: Then free cash flow, and how much new debt they sell.
lines.say: Then come the other two: free cash flow, and how much new debt these companies sell to pay for the build.

lines.text: Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet rent AI computing to other businesses, so cloud sales are one early place a payoff would show.
lines.say: Cloud sales matter because Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet rent AI computing to other businesses. That's one of the first places a payoff would show.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap
lines.say: Let's wrap it up.

lines.text: Meta's AI spending passed its operating cash, and Big Tech borrowing is more than 4x its old pace.
lines.say: Quick recap. Meta's AI spending passed the cash its business brought in, and Big Tech bond sales run at more than four times their old pace.

lines.text: The 1990s showed a real technology can still burn its backers. And index funds already own a slice of this bet.
lines.say: The nineties showed a real technology can still burn its backers. And an index fund already owns a slice of this bet.

lines.text: The bill is due now. The payoff isn't here yet. The next two weeks of earnings will tell us a lot.
lines.say: The bill is due now. The payoff isn't here yet. The next two weeks of earnings will tell us a lot more.

lines.text: Subscribe for the week's biggest money story, every Friday.
lines.say: If this helped, subscribe, and I'll see you next Friday for the week's biggest money story.

post.title: Meta's AI bill is now bigger than its cash. Big Tech's $700B spending boom, explained
post.ig: Meta's AI spending passed the cash its business brought in. Here's Big Tech's $700B AI bill, the 1990s fiber lesson, and what it means for index funds.
post.tiktok: Meta's AI bill is now bigger than the cash it makes. Big Tech's AI spending boom, explained.
post.yt_desc:
Meta spent $34.91B on capex from July to September 2026, more than the $32.79B its business brought in, so its free cash flow turned negative. Tesla's research spending jumped 69% while profit fell 43%, and SpaceX's AI unit became its biggest seller while Starlink earned most of the profit. This video explains how big Big Tech's AI bill is, how borrowing is rising, what the late-1990s telecom and fiber boom teaches, who wins and who pays, and what it means for index fund and 401(k) holders, plus the earnings dates to watch.

News and education, not financial advice.
